speaker: Brad Smith
title: An interview with Microsoft President Brad Smith
question: In software liability and governance, why do governments hold cloud AI providers more accountable for downstream misuse than traditional packaged-software vendors?
guest: There is a second dimension that is, to some degree, at odds with the notion of providing this technology to anyone who wants it to do with it whatever they choose. You can't empower people if you can't protect them and keep them safe. So there are certain use cases that we won't allow for our technology, and at times there are certain countries where we won't be comfortable providing the full range of services. This is vastly more complicated than the world of producing Microsoft Word and letting anybody use it, knowing that somebody would create a work that would get the Nobel Prize in Literature and someone else would write something truly horrible. We created the tool, and we were not responsible for whether somebody turned it into a weapon, because we couldn't control that. But in a world where AI runs as a service in a data center from the cloud, you can impose more controls. That is one of the reasons governments and the public are expecting more of tech companies. They expect us to do more because we can and should.

points.core: Packaged software vendors lacked technical control over downstream misuse after shipping.
points.note: Accept: once local tools like word processors were sold, makers could not monitor or block how buyers used them. Do not credit: claiming older software was less dangerous without noting the vendor's lack of post-sale control.

points.core: Running AI continuously in cloud data centers gives providers ongoing operational control.
points.note: Accept: hosted cloud delivery lets providers technically enforce guardrails, monitor usage, or restrict access in real time. Do not credit: vague statements that AI is powerful without tying accountability to cloud-hosted architecture.

points.core: Cloud providers can directly restrict prohibited use cases across specific customer jurisdictions.
points.note: Accept: providers can refuse to serve certain use cases, limit feature availability in certain countries, or enforce acceptable-use boundaries. Do not credit: generic claims that companies should be responsible without noting selective restriction capability.

points.core: Greater technical ability to intervene drives higher legal expectations from the public.
points.note: Accept: governments and society demand more enforcement from tech firms specifically because cloud architecture makes intervention technically feasible. Do not credit: generic anti-Big-Tech sentiment unrelated to technical controllability.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core reason is control: a cloud AI provider keeps an ongoing, operational relationship with every use of its product, while a packaged-software vendor loses control at the point of sale.

Traditional software ships as a finished copy that runs on the customer's own machines. The vendor cannot see what it is used for, cannot intervene, and typically disclaims liability through licence terms, so the law has treated it much like a tool-maker and placed responsibility on the user.

Cloud AI is delivered as a continuing service. The provider hosts the model, processes each request, can log and monitor usage, enforce acceptable-use policies, verify customers, throttle or cut off access, and retrain or patch the system. That capacity to foresee, detect and stop misuse supports a duty of care, since liability tends to follow knowledge and control, and the provider is often the cheapest party to prevent harm.

Two further factors reinforce this. General-purpose AI is highly dual-use and scalable, and its outputs are generated by the provider's own system rather than authored by the user. Regulations such as the EU AI Act and proposed know-your-customer rules for cloud compute reflect this logic.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Governments hold cloud AI providers more accountable than traditional packaged-software vendors primarily because cloud delivery preserves ongoing visibility and operational control. Once packaged software ships, vendors lose sight of local deployments and cannot intervene against abuse. By contrast, cloud AI runs continuously on the provider’s own infrastructure, enabling vendors to detect anomalous usage, update safety guardrails, filter harmful outputs, and revoke access in real time. In liability doctrine, this continuous agency makes the provider the "least-cost avoider" best positioned to mitigate downstream harm.

Furthermore, general-purpose AI changes both the nature of software risk and the practicality of enforcement. Unlike deterministic programs that merely execute explicit user commands, frontier models actively synthesize capabilities—such as tailored malware, mass fraud, or hazardous designs—lowering technical barriers for bad actors at scale. Because massive compute and capital requirements concentrate model hosting among a handful of firms rather than millions of dispersed end users, upstream cloud providers serve as natural regulatory chokepoints where safety governance is actually enforceable.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The main reason is control. A traditional packaged-software vendor ships a product and then mostly loses sight of it. It can't see how buyers use it, can't step in when something goes wrong, and has long relied on license disclaimers to limit liability. A cloud AI provider keeps operating the system after the sale. Every request passes through its servers, so it can monitor usage, enforce acceptable-use policies, filter outputs, rate-limit, suspend accounts, and patch the model for all users at once. Regulators generally place duties on whoever is best placed to prevent harm cheaply, and that ongoing ability to act makes a fault argument based on "they knew or could have known" much easier to make.

Other factors add to this. General-purpose models carry dual-use risks, such as help with cyberattacks or bio threats, that weren't designed for one specific use. A single provider serves millions of users, so one failure can spread widely. And the provider is a concentrated, identifiable party that's easier to regulate than scattered end users. The EU AI Act's obligations for general-purpose AI models and safety commitments from frontier labs reflect this thinking.

Liability in this area is still unsettled, though, and the gap is narrowing. The EU's revised Product Liability Directive now covers software in general, including packaged software.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Governments hold cloud AI providers more accountable than traditional packaged-software vendors primarily because of ongoing operational control, visibility, and regulatory leverage. When a vendor sells packaged software, the code runs locally on the buyer's machine, leaving the vendor largely blind to downstream use and unable to intervene without the user's cooperation. By contrast, cloud AI operates as a continuously hosted service on the provider's infrastructure. Providers process every prompt and output, making them active participants in generating results rather than passive sellers of a static tool. This architecture gives them the technical ability to monitor for abuse, apply safety filters, update model behavior centrally, and immediately suspend malicious accounts.

From a governance perspective, cloud providers also serve as the "least-cost avoiders" and most enforceable chokepoints. Because general-purpose AI can rapidly scale harms like fraud, cyberattacks, or illicit content across millions of anonymous users, regulators find it far more practical—and legally justified—to require safeguards from a small number of centralized providers who profit continuously from that usage.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Governments often expect more from cloud AI providers because they retain control over the service after customers start using it. A provider can detect patterns of abuse, enforce usage limits, update safeguards, and suspend accounts. A single hosted model can also enable misuse at scale, making intervention by the provider more practical than pursuing individual users.

Packaged-software vendors generally have less visibility into how customers use installed copies and fewer ways to intervene once the software ships. Their obligations tend to center on product defects, security updates, and warnings. For cloud AI, governance can also address how the provider operates the service day to day and responds to foreseeable misuse. The legal duties vary by jurisdiction and can be shared with the organizations that deploy the AI and the people who use it.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Governments often place greater duties on cloud AI providers because those providers retain control after deployment. A provider can update a model, limit access to risky capabilities, or suspend an account after receiving a credible abuse report. A vendor that sells software for customers to run locally usually has less visibility into how they use it and less ability to intervene. A cloud provider can also reduce a foreseeable risk across many customers through a single change to its service.

The distinction matters because a duty to take reasonable precautions is easier to justify when a company can recognize a risk and act on it. That does not make the provider automatically liable for a customer’s misconduct. Legal responsibility depends on the jurisdiction, the provider’s role, what it knew or reasonably could have foreseen, and the steps it could reasonably have taken.
